en: Your devastating elder, Khan Bakai,
Reached Közkaman.
The panther, when he reached him,
That very warrior Közkaman's
Head he cut off as he passed.
Shrill cries, fierce cheering—
Do not ask about the tale!
The mighty warrior Kökchököz
Lashed his blue rhinoceros:
“They were merely half-Mongol dogs!
Let me reach these Buruts,
And of that strayed Chinese,
Almambet, cut off the head.
Chubak, Bakai, Almambet—
I shall throw them all into turmoil
And wipe them out.
Fighting another forty days,
I shall thus bring them to their end.
Having let my kinsman Közkaman be killed,
How could I go away alive?
Until the supple reed ripens,
Until the gossamer's ash takes flight,
Fighting hard for six months,
I shall kill the forty companions.
Driving them, crushing them,
To Khan Manas, who has brought us grief,
I shall thrust them right beneath him!”
As though an evil spirit had seized his wife,
As though all his courage had fled,
His ribs coming apart,
The tears of that unbeliever
Poured down below his collarbone.
Grieving without sparing his life,
Bereft of his own brother Közkaman,
He entered the battle in earnest.
Mounted upon Aisarala,
Almambet was nearly reached;
Drawing within an arrow's flight,
As the spear was stretched to strike,
Shrill cries, fierce cheering—
Akbaltai's Chubak
Shouted and raised his spear.
Striking Kökala on the flank,
Before he could reach Khan Almambet,
He attacked Kökchököz
And arrived before an arrow could.
Chubak, when he reached him,
From atop the blue rhinoceros
Brought him crashing down as he passed.
Roaring in fury,
Kökchököz flew from his mount,
Crying “Beijing!” as his battle-cry,
His wings broken,
Parted from his blue rhinoceros.
Almambet the lion, the noble lion,
Took Zhoykuma in hand
And stretched out his sword there.
That great club-like lock of hair
My generous, expert Almambet
Seized and twisted in his grasp.
Before a word could be spoken,
He cut off his head.
Dragging him onto the road,
He ripped him open for the dogs.
As though drinking kumiss,
Your precious, outstanding Syrgak
Took Kökchököz's dark blood,
Scooping and sipping with both hands,
And swallowed draught after draught.
His burning heart was soothed,
All his anguish eased.
Generous Sultan Manas's
Vengeance was taken thus.
Against those who remained, Khan Bakai
Launched a crushing attack.
Letting not a single one escape,
He slaughtered them thus.
Kökchököz and Közkaman—
They slew both in turn.
Not one of their Kalmyks remained;
They killed them all.
Crushed to meal upon the plain,
Such suffering they endured.
The villains' countless plundered gold
They loaded to take back to Talas.
To wounded Manas the wolf-man,
The brass spyglass with its turning screw
Grasping it by a corner and turning it,
With six swift horses,
With a letter the size of a palm,
They sent the servant Shuutu.
Traveling day and night,
Hastening along the road,
He crossed Suusamyr,
Passed over Kötörmö.
Exultant in his daring,
To hero Sultan Manas
The servant Shuutu brought glad tidings,
Met him and gave his news.
Bowing, Shuutu spoke:
“My generous Manas, to you, Khan,
Allah has granted a gift, I say.
Your burning pain is soothed, Manas;
All your anguish is relieved, Manas.
The fugitives camped at the ford, Manas;
The moment you needed has come, Manas.
The fugitives camped at Jyldyz, Manas;
A joyful path has opened for you, Manas.
Your kinsman with the sweet kumiss, Manas,
The mighty heroes have slain, Manas.
Those who left you camped at the ford, Manas;
The moment you needed has come, Manas.
That swaggering elder brother Közkaman, Manas,
Khan Bakai has hacked down, Manas.
Almambet fought with shots, Manas;
Your mighty, outstanding Chubak, Manas,
Reached him from behind the shoulder, Manas.
Your imposing elder Kökchököz, Manas,
Flew from his rhinoceros, Manas.
Your lion Almambet, blessed by Khidr, Manas,
Has thus brought him to his end, Manas.
Syrgak gouged him from outside, Manas.
Your kinsmen who came from the Kalmyks, Manas,
The forty companions have slaughtered, Manas!”
Dipping his hands in water,
Khan Manas, sitting motionless,
Performed his ritual hand-washing.
The noble lion sobbed and wept,
Then pleaded with the servant Shuutu:
“If my brow thus clears, my Shuutu,
If my burning heart is soothed, my Shuutu,
I shall not begrudge a hair of my wealth, my Shuutu.
If this news of yours is true, my Shuutu,
You have kindled an extinguished fire, my Shuutu,
You have revived a dead soul, my Shuutu.
By building I made a house, my Shuutu;
By planting you forty companions I made a garden, my Shuutu.
I took you with me, made you a hero, my Shuutu.
Forty mighty men come from every land, my Shuutu—
I made you equal to a hero's son, my Shuutu.
If this news of yours is true, my Shuutu,
Take my Kyrgyz village in Talas, my Shuutu.
Leave my child and take my wife, my Shuutu.
Leave my file and take my whetstone, my Shuutu.
Leave my queen Kanykei beside me, my Shuutu;
Take the two, beginning with Akylai, my Shuutu.
Take my house built in Talas, my Shuutu.
Leave my body and take my soul, my Shuutu.
Take my myriad livestock on the hills, my Shuutu.
If that is too little, take my blood poured into a leather flask, my Shuutu.
Leave my otters and take my foxes, my Shuutu.
I shall give it all without a thought, my Shuutu.
Take my possessions, beginning with my treasury, my Shuutu!
That noble sister-in-law of yours, Kanykei,
Spent my wealth
And saved my life, which was being wasted away.
Thoroughbreds and coursers together,
Fine horses upon the hills,
Bring the broad-humped camels.
Cut them open, my hero Shuutu,
And hundreds of crescent-hoofed mares.
Do not spare my livestock.
Slaughter mares in honor
Of my life delivered from death.
I have no courser left to mount by the neck,
Nor have I a brother from my own nest
With whom to share death.”
Then, in the hollow of Jylgynduu,
Along broad Talas,
Thinking he would die.
Argyn and Ogoy gathered,
Feasting for sixty days.
They settled along broad Talas;
Argyn and Kyrgyz mingled,
Doing as they pleased.
Khan Manas's forty mighty men
Had let no fugitives escape:
This was the time they caught and delivered them.
Kökchököz and Közkaman—
Both had been put into the grave;
Today they returned after killing them.
Every beak had grown strong,
Every enemy was worn away.
Their wings had grown a span;
All rejoiced in the heroes.
Offering prayers to Baabedin,
To Allah the Exalted, the One,
They vowed crescent-hoofed horses.
What was severed was joined,
What was scattered was gathered.
From the battle with Közkaman,
Ajybai and Khan Bakai were safe,
Almambet and Chubak the lions were safe,
Serek and Syrgak both were safe,
The elder Ulukman was safe,
All Manas's forty noble companions were safe.
The strength on which they relied was safe,
Their fortified place was safe,
The renowned elder Bakai was safe,
All the champions were safe.
Argyn and Kyrgyz together,
Their noble heads winning honor,
Those slaughtering mares slew mares;
Those slaughtering camels slew camels.
Breaking sugar like snow,
Heaping up golden butter,
Spreading their wealth abroad,
Fattened lambs, delicious heads,
They boiled in bubbling pots.
Even death would bring no regret.
When Közkaman was brought,
They held a feast for sixty days,
Argyn and Kyrgyz gathered.
Whole otter skins
They divided into halves
And put upon their trouser cuffs.
Gnawing sugar like snow,
Drinking liquor like water,
Wearing paired marten-fur caps,
Swaying aside on their own,
With no one left to contradict them,
Each man was himself a lord,
Delighting in being a sultan.
His tiger bore fifteen young;
No one dared approach,
They matched the heroes.
Khan Manas came forth in Talas;
His wrath drove souls from bodies.
He drove gray deer and made them cattle;
Every place he set his sights upon
He devastated and threw into turmoil.
He drove white deer and made them cattle;
Every place where battle was joined
Your father took and threw into turmoil.
Kokand used to inflict oppression;
From Alty-Shaar and Kokand
Six thousand silver ingots, a thousand otter skins,
He took as tribute.
Your father Manas, the generous lion,
Would not listen when I spoke,
Calling that blind wretch his kinsman.
Deceived by the villain, he drank poison,
Pierced in forty places,
Unconscious forty days, unable to speak,
Suffering, he barely became human again.
I, your luckless mother,
Made a warrior of my woman's self,
Made a banner of my towering head,
Rescued your father,
Raised a tumult against the villains.
He made me bear such hardship;
Your witless father would not listen.
My breasts were split with wounds—
What misery did I not endure!
Because of your father, the Lion,
How many calamities I have borne!
